source.title: Emergent phases of superposition: from partial to full representation
source.authors: Li-Hao Guo; Yizhou Liu; Jeff Gore

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures loss scaling in a trained toy network and finds different width-loss behavior on either side of a representation transition, qualifying how broadly one power-law form can be expected to apply.
record.gate_note: The study trains Anthropic's toy model of superposition and measures mean-square reconstruction loss, not held-out cross-entropy in language-model pretraining. It does not sweep language-model parameters, tokens, or compute, test extrapolation, or find a compute-optimal allocation. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains Anthropic's toy model of superposition on synthetic sparse inputs and measures mean-square reconstruction loss against hidden width m at fixed feature count n. This is not language-model pretraining loss (V1–V4, V6, V7). It is also not a model in another modality or training regime such as image, video, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer (V5). Width is swept at a single n (n = 10000 shown). Data and compute are not scaled, and no power-law exponent is fitted across orders of magnitude. The 1/m decay above the critical width, and the slow decay with a bend below it, are a mechanistic toy-model account of width scaling. They are a related construct, not a test of any version, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. The record's V5 labels, one supports and one challenges, are therefore removed.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but incomplete. Increasing width drives a continuous transition from partial to full representation, with critical width m* ∼ Ē log(n/Ē). Below m*, loss grows linearly in Ē and depends weakly on width. Above m*, it grows roughly quadratically in Ē and decays as 1/m. Non-uniform firing delays the transition and lowers the loss. The authors note that extension to other architectures and losses is unverified. They present this as a step toward understanding representation scaling in large models.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a sparse-feature embedding/unembedding toy network and measures mean-square reconstruction loss while varying width and data statistics. It does not use language-model pretraining, held-out cross-entropy, or parameter-token-compute scaling sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss and transition depend on width regime and data statistics, including mean active-feature count, non-uniform firing probabilities, activation variance, and feature-activation variability.

fits_no_version.finding: In the toy superposition model, loss decays slowly with width below a critical width m* (partial representation) and approximately as 1/m above it, with a bend in the L–m curve around m*.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In sparse-feature toy models, the width scaling of loss changes form at a partial-to-full representation transition; inverse-width scaling holds only above the critical width.

fits_no_version.finding: The critical width grows as Ē log(n/Ē), and grows further with non-uniform firing probabilities and with variability of the active-feature count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The width at which loss enters inverse-width scaling is set by data sparsity statistics.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss grows roughly linearly in Ē below m* and quadratically (up to a log) above it. Non-uniform firing lowers loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this toy model, the loss prefactor depends on feature activity statistics as well as width.

record.problems: The evidence concerns a toy network and mean-square reconstruction loss, not language-model pretraining cross-entropy. The authors note reliance on the linear representation hypothesis, approximations to crosstalk noise, and that extension to other architectures and losses remains unverified. Seed-to-seed errors were too small to see in figures and error bars were omitted in most figures.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported loss-scaling results were omitted. Representation-parameter distributions and geometric measurements are not rows because they do not measure the loss behavior named in the claim; cited results from other studies are excluded.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss; no parameter, token or compute sweep.
No comparison of shapes at fixed parameter count.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer setting. The synthetic toy autoencoder is not treated as such a regime.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices across setups. The bend in the L–m curve concerns toy MSE, not language-model loss.

record.verdict_notes: The authors cite Liu et al. (2025) and related LLM work for inverse-width scaling in real LLMs; those are cited results, not rows. Appendix C reports effects of σv and σE on loss and m* (Figs. 11, 20, 21), which also fit no version. Training details: n ranged 1000–65536, but only n = 10000 is shown, with m ranging 10–16384. Seed-to-seed errors were reported as negligible.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss in language models or sweep parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens is tested.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
It tests a toy-network training setting with reconstruction loss only; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or language-model pretraining.
No downstream task performance is measured.

The study does not compare fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices. It does report a width-loss curve that bends around a transition, but for a toy model rather than held-out language-model pretraining loss.

rows.subject: Anthropic's toy model of superposition
rows.stage_stated: Trained for 3 × 10^4 steps on the input ensemble
rows.operation_detail: Varied model width m and measured reconstruction loss L
rows.value: Before the transition, L decays slowly with m; the L-m curve bends around m*.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this result; the paper reports that seed-to-seed errors were too small to see in its figures.
rows.note: The stated loss is toy-model mean-square error, not held-out cross-entropy.
rows.check: Toy-model MSE loss vs width on synthetic sparse data, not loss of a model in another modality or training regime, so it does not bear on V5. The 'partial' state was judged against V5. As a finding, the slow decay below m* is observed (Fig. 2c). Loss values are only given graphically.

rows.subject: Anthropic's toy model of superposition
rows.stage_stated: Trained for 3 × 10^4 steps on the input ensemble
rows.operation_detail: Varied mean number of active features Ē and measured the critical width m*
rows.measure: Critical width m* for transition to full representation
rows.value: m* grows asymptotically as Ē log(n/Ē) in the limit 1 ≪ Ē ≪ n; experiments are reported as consistent with the prediction.
rows.note: This is a representation-transition result, not a compute-optimal allocation.

rows.subject: Anthropic's toy model of superposition
rows.stage_stated: Trained for 3 × 10^4 steps on the input ensemble
rows.operation_detail: Varied mean number of active features Ē and measured reconstruction loss L
rows.measure: Mean-square reconstruction loss L as a function of Ē
rows.value: L ≈ (Ē/n)(v̄² + σv²); the loss grows linearly with Ē in this regime.
rows.note: The expression is stated for the small-width regime.

rows.subject: Anthropic's toy model of superposition
rows.stage_stated: Trained for 3 × 10^4 steps on the input ensemble
rows.operation_detail: Varied mean number of active features Ē and measured reconstruction loss L
rows.measure: Mean-square reconstruction loss L as a function of Ē
rows.value: L ≈ (2σv² Ē²/(nm)) log(n/Ē); the loss grows approximately quadratically in Ē up to a logarithmic correction.
rows.note: The expression is stated for the full-representation regime.

rows.value: The loss decreases as ϵp increases.
rows.note: The authors attribute the decrease to more frequent features occupying more hidden dimensions.
